citation: Buckley FP, Duval Neto G, Fink BR. Acid and alkaline solutions of local anesthetics: duration of nerve block and tissue pH. Anesth Analg 1985;64:477-482
found_in_paper: S-686-04 reference 8, cited on page 4 as the regional-nerve-block leg of the sentence that studies have shown the duration of anaesthetic effect is unchanged by buffering
what_it_shows: A double-blind study of rat infraorbital nerve blocks which found that the pH of the injected solution had little or no effect on how long the block lasted, and which measured tissue pH with a microelectrode after injection. It is an animal nerve-block experiment, not a human study and not in skin. It matters because it is the strongest of the three references behind Christoph 1988's duration sentence, and so behind any reading of Christoph's abstract as evidence about duration: once this is seen, Christoph's 'duration of skin anesthesia was not altered' is a restatement of a rat nerve-block result and not a measurement made in human skin. Looked up on Europe PMC (engine europepmc, query EXT_ID-free title plus author search, 2026-10-08, hitCount 1).
quote_from_abstract: Injectable pH had little or no effect upon the duration of block.

citation: DiFazio CA, Carron H, Grosslight KR, Moscicki JC, Bolding WR, Johns RA. Comparison of pH-adjusted lidocaine solutions for epidural anesthesia. Anesth Analg 1986;65:760-764
found_in_paper: S-686-04 reference 10, cited on page 4 as one of the two major-nerve-block references for the same unchanged-duration sentence, and on page 2 among the studies said to have focused on efficacy after pH adjustment
what_it_shows: 148 adult patients having epidural anaesthesia, assigned to five solutions of differing measured pH. The endpoints it reports are onset of analgesia and onset of surgical anaesthesia, both faster in the pH-adjusted groups; the abstract reports no duration result at all and the route is epidural, not cutaneous. So the second leg of Christoph 1988's duration support is an onset study in a different compartment. Looked up on Europe PMC (engine europepmc, title search, 2026-10-08, hitCount 1).
quote_from_abstract: Times of onset of analgesia … were significantly more rapid in the groups that received the pH-adjusted solutions

citation: Cunningham NL, Kaplan JA. A rapid-onset, long-acting regional anesthetic technique. Anesthesiology 1974;41:509-511
found_in_paper: S-686-14 (Kim 1979), reference 1 and the worked example in its introduction, page 1
what_it_shows: A human comparison, five years before Kim 1979, of a chloroprocaine-plus-bupivacaine mixture against bupivacaine alone in brachial plexus block, reporting mean duration of motor blockade for each - the mixture's the shorter of the two. It is a published pre-1979 study of an ester and an amide given together, with block duration as the outcome, which is exactly what C033 says nobody had studied. Route is brachial plexus, not skin, so it leaves Kim 1979 as the first intradermal answer.

citation: Raj PP, Rosenblatt R, Miller J, Katz RL, Carden E. Dynamics of local-anesthetic compounds in regional anesthesia. Anesth Analg 1977;56(1):110-117
found_in_paper: S-686-14 (Kim 1979), reference 11, discussed on page 3
what_it_shows: A second pre-1979 human study of the same ester-plus-amide mixture, in the paper's own reference list: compounded mixtures of chloroprocaine plus bupivacaine (and of lidocaine plus bupivacaine) given for epidural or brachial plexus block in 48 adult patients. Like Cunningham 1974 it matches every element C033 says is absent except the intradermal route, so the two together refute 'a question nobody had answered'. Kim cites it for its plasma-level finding rather than for duration.
quote_from_abstract: The clinical effectiveness and safety of compounded mixtures of lidocaine + bupivacaine and chloroprocaine + bupivacaine for either epidural or brachial-plexus block was studied in 48 adult patients.

citation: Defalque RJ, Stoelting VK. Latency and duration of action of some local anesthetic mixtures. Anesth Analg 1966;45:106-116
found_in_paper: S-686-14 (Kim 1979), reference 2, summarised in its introduction, page 1
what_it_shows: A 1966 study of local anaesthetic mixtures measuring latency and duration, summarised by Kim as the work in which an ester (tetracaine) was added to procaine or to lidocaine and epidural duration tracked in dogs, with the result depending on how much tetracaine the mixture held. Supports C033's refutation by showing that mixtures of a long-acting and a short-acting agent, and their effect on duration, were an established subject before 1979; the population is animal and the route epidural, so it does not match C033's human element on its own.

citation: Luduena FP. Duration of local anesthesia. Annu Rev Pharmacol 1969;9:503-519
found_in_paper: S-686-14 (Kim 1979), reference 10, discussed on page 3; Cited twice in the discussion of S-686-25 as the source for prolongation of intradermal action by inherent vasoconstrictor activity in the optical isomers of bupivacaine, mepivacaine and prilocaine, and for the vasoconstrictor activity of the dental agents.
what_it_shows: Reported by Kim as finding that intradermal block by a long-acting agent (propoxycaine) in guinea pigs was significantly shortened when a short-acting ester (procaine) was added - the same route and the same direction of effect as Kim 1979, in animals, ten years earlier. Relevant background for any statement that nothing had looked at whether mixing shortens an intradermal block. No abstract is on record and the primary paper was not read.

citation: Collins JB, Song J, Mahabir RC. Onset and duration of intradermal mixtures of bupivacaine and lidocaine with epinephrine. Can J Plast Surg 2013;21(1):51-53
found_in_paper: Not cited by S-686-14 (it postdates it); found in the paper's forward-citation list, and already in the record's own bupivacaine-wheals register
what_it_shows: A human intradermal mixing study in the same tissue and by the same route as Kim 1979, but amide with amide: 25 subjects, randomised and double-blind, four intradermal forearm injections each, onset and duration of four bupivacaine/lidocaine-with-epinephrine mixtures timed by sharp skin prick. Bears on the Ropivacaine page's claim that Kim 1979 is 'the only one in the right tissue by the right route' (notion finding F008), and on C040's account of whether Sweet's comparison has been repeated.
quote_from_abstract: Twenty-five subjects were enrolled in a double-blinded, randomized block design study to evaluate the onset and duration of four different mixtures of lidocaine and bupivacaine with epinephrine.

citation: Peterfreund RA, Datta S, Ostheimer GW. pH adjustment of local anesthetic solutions with sodium bicarbonate: laboratory evaluation of alkalinization and precipitation. Regional Anesthesia 1989;14(6):265-270. DOI 10.1136/rapm-00115550-198914060-00002
found_in_paper: Milner 2000 reference 1, where the first author's surname is misprinted as 'Petertreund'. Looked up and verified independently (engine: europepmc, query title:"pH adjustment of local anesthetic solutions with sodium bicarbonate", hitCount 6, the 1989 record retrieved as PMID 2562097).
what_it_shows: The bench study Milner set out to replace with a single method, and already the source behind the bupivacaine-wheals page's 'it cannot be brought to body pH' passage. It establishes the per-drug split: 2-chloroprocaine and lidocaine take bicarbonate to near physiological pH without precipitating, mepivacaine precipitates with a latency of 18-20 minutes above neutral pH at [dose figure omitted], and bupivacaine and etidocaine precipitate after small additions and cannot be brought to physiologic pH. It decides neither D017 nor D018: it has no ropivacaine arm (ropivacaine was not in clinical use in 1989), no human subjects and no pain outcome. Recorded for two reasons - it is the methodological parent of both Milner 2000 and the record's bupivacaine passage, and it carries a latency finding (delayed precipitation at 18-20 minutes in a different amide) that is the same phenomenon Fulling & Peterfreund 2000 later measured in ropivacaine, which is what makes the observation window the decisive variable in D017.
quote_from_abstract: Bupivacaine and etidocaine solutions precipitated after the addition of small amounts of sodium bicarbonate and could not be alkalinized to physiologic pH.

citation: Bourget P, Bonhomme L, Benhamou D. Factors influencing precipitation of pH-adjusted bupivacaine solutions. Journal of Clinical Pharmacy and Therapeutics 1990;15:197-204 (Milner 2000 ref. 12, where the third author is printed 'Benhmou'); and Bonhomme L, Benhamou D, Jebri M, Bourget P, Matre H, Postaire E, Preaux N. Chemical stability of bupivacaine in pH-adjusted solutions. Anesthesiology 1988;69:754-756 (ref. 13)
found_in_paper: Milner 2000 references 12 and 13, cited in its Discussion (p. 41) as the particle-counter studies that qualify its own null precipitation result. Not looked up individually: Europe PMC was used for the ropivacaine-specific records that could decide D017, and neither of these has a ropivacaine arm, so neither can.
what_it_shows: Milner reports that these two found particle counts rising after alkalinization of similar solutions to pH above 7, where its own naked-eye and microscopic inspection, before and after centrifugation, found nothing. That is a methodological point rather than a verdict: it means an 'absence of visible precipitate' finding - the outcome element of D017 - depends on how hard the observer looked, and that both Ramos 2001's optical microscopy and Milner's own microscopy sit above the detection floor a particle counter would set. Neither study involves ropivacaine, so neither decides D017 or D018.

citation: Howe NR, Williams JM. Pain of injection and duration of anesthesia for intradermal infiltration of lidocaine, bupivacaine, and etidocaine. J Dermatol Surg Oncol 1994;20(7):459-464. DOI 10.1111/j.1524-4725.1994.tb03216.x
found_in_paper: Not cited by S-686-17 (S-686-17 is from 1975). Identified as 'the one that is cited' from the Notion bupivacaine-wheals, comparison and 'still unsettled' pages, then fetched and verified independently (engine: europepmc, query EXT_ID:8034840).
what_it_shows: This, not Morgan & Russell 1975, is the paper the record cites for the intradermal injection-pain ranking in which etidocaine comes out worst. Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blinded, 20 subjects, intradermal etidocaine, bupivacaine and lidocaine [dose figures omitted] plus normal saline, each with and without epinephrine, every solution adjusted to pH 5.95 +/- 0.15. Its ordering is as the record states it. Europe PMC confirms the authors, year, journal, pages 459-464 and the abstract wording; full text subscription-only, so the millimetre values remain unread, exactly as the record says.
quote_from_abstract: Lidocaine hurt least and etidocaine hurt most. Adrenalized solutions were more painful than plain. For plain solutions bupivacaine lasted longest and lidocaine lasted shortest by far.

citation: Geddes IC. Local anaesthetic properties and toxicity of hydroxyprocaine and hydroxyamethocaine. Br J Anaesth 1956;28(2):55-66. DOI 10.1093/bja/28.2.55
found_in_paper: Reference list and introduction of S-686-17, p. 586, cited as one of the two earlier uses of the intradermal weal technique in man
what_it_shows: Cannot be established from available records. Europe PMC holds the citation but no abstract (engine: europepmc, query AUTH:"Geddes IC" AND SRC:MED AND PUB_YEAR:1956; hitCount 2); the only content is MeSH - Anesthetics Local, Anesthesia Local, Procaine/analogs & derivatives - and the full text is subscription-only. All that is established is that Morgan & Russell cite it as a human intradermal weal study. Because hydroxyamethocaine is an amethocaine (tetracaine) analogue, it is worth opening against D045's claim that Willatts holds the only human intradermal timing of tetracaine, but it cannot decide that claim from here, and the analogue is not tetracaine itself.

citation: Sinha HK. The local anesthetic actions of certain pyrazoline and quinoline compounds. J Pharmacol Exp Ther 1936;57:199
found_in_paper: Reference list and introduction of S-686-17, p. 586, cited as the earlier use of the intradermal weal technique in man
what_it_shows: Not retrievable. No matching record in Europe PMC (engine: europepmc, query AUTH:"Sinha HK" OR (TITLE:"pyrazoline" AND TITLE:"anesthetic") - 14 hits, none this paper; 1936 J Pharmacol Exp Ther appears not to be indexed). It is recorded here only because it dates human intradermal weal testing to 1936, which is earlier than the 1952 start the Notion wheal-literature page gives that tradition.

citation: Eriksson E. L 67 - experimental evaluation of a new local anaesthetic in man. Acta Anaesthesiologica Scandinavica 1961;5:191-205. DOI 10.1111/j.1399-6576.1961.tb00095.x
found_in_paper: S-686-20 (Padfield 1967), reference 2, and discussed in the introduction on p1
what_it_shows: An experimental evaluation of prilocaine in man that, on Padfield's account, repeated the 1959 figures and extended the longer-duration claim to finger, caudal and spinal blocks. If it contains intradermal duration data it would be an earlier human intradermal timing of prilocaine than Reynolds 1976 or Willatts 1985. Europe PMC holds the record with no abstract and subscription-only full text, so what it measured could not be read in this session; it is logged here as a lead, not as evidence. Cited 11 times.

citation: Eriksson E, Gordh T. Clinical trials of a new local anaesthetic. Acta Anaesthesiologica Scandinavica 1959;Suppl 12:81
found_in_paper: S-686-20 (Padfield 1967), reference 1, and the opening sentences on p1
what_it_shows: The original claim that prilocaine has a longer intradermal duration of action than lignocaine. Padfield reports that this claim rested on findings which did not reach statistical significance. Not found in Europe PMC (searched by author and title; it is a supplement and appears not to be indexed), so it has no PMID here and could not be read.

citation: Mongar JL. A study of two methods for testing local anaesthetics in man. British Journal of Pharmacology and Chemotherapy 1955;10(2):240-246. PMC1509502. DOI 10.1111/j.1476-5381.1955.tb00089.x
found_in_paper: S-686-20 (Padfield 1967), reference 13; the class experiment design was adapted from it
what_it_shows: The method source for Padfield's design: a 1955 human study comparing two methods for testing local anaesthetics in man. If one of the two methods is an intradermal weal with timed testing, it would be the earliest human intradermal local-anaesthetic testing study in this set and could bear on which procaine intradermal data exist. It has no abstract, and its free full text could not be retrieved in this session: both europepmc.org and onlinelibrary.wiley.com are denied by the egress proxy (CONNECT 403), and the Europe PMC fullTextXML endpoint returns a 500 for this record. Logged as an unresolved lead. Cited 6 times.

citation: Purnell RJ, Frew RM, Roth IZ. The topical analgesic action of prilocaine. A comparison with lignocaine by two methods. Anaesthesia 1966;21(4):480-489. DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2044.1966.tb02653.x
found_in_paper: S-686-20 (Padfield 1967), reference 9, and the introduction on p1
what_it_shows: A randomised comparative clinical trial of topical prilocaine against lignocaine by two methods, which Padfield reports as finding durations similar for the two agents. Topical and by MeSH applied to larynx and trachea, not intradermal, so it does not reach the intradermal wheal claims. Note that Padfield's reference list omits the third author (Roth). No abstract.

citation: Thornton JA. Recent advances in local analgesia. Clinical experience with prilocaine. Proceedings of the Royal Society of Medicine 1965;58:418-420. PMC1898583. DOI 10.1177/003591576505800610
found_in_paper: S-686-20 (Padfield 1967), reference 8, and the introduction on p1
what_it_shows: The other of the two topical prilocaine-versus-lignocaine reports Padfield cites as reaching opposing conclusions; Padfield reports this one as suggesting prilocaine lasted longer. Clinical experience across bronchoscopy, conduction and obstetric anaesthesia, not an intradermal study, so it does not decide any wheal claim. Free full text in Europe PMC. No abstract.

citation: von Bahr V, Eriksson E. Citanest (L 67) - ett nytt lokalanestesimedel. Svenska Lakartidningen 1962;59:2221-2232
found_in_paper: S-686-20 (Padfield 1967), reference 6, and the introduction on p1
what_it_shows: Padfield's source for the statement that prilocaine outlasted lignocaine in peripheral nerve, spinal and epidural blockade but that the two lasted alike once a vasoconstrictor was added to each. That is a vasoconstrictor-and-duration observation, but by nerve-block and neuraxial routes rather than intradermally, so it does not reach the intradermal scope of D023 or D054. In Swedish, no abstract.

citation: Fulling PD, Peterfreund RA. Alkalinization and precipitation characteristics of 0.2% ropivacaine. Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine 2000;25(5):518-521. DOI 10.1053/rapm.2000.8931
found_in_paper: Ramos 2001 reference 11, discussed on its p. 361. Verified independently (engine: europepmc, query EXT_ID:11009239).
what_it_shows: The direct counterpart to Ramos on D017, and already in the claim's records_read. Three things matter now that both full texts have been read. First, Ramos miscites it: Ramos gives the ropivacaine strength as ten times the strength Fulling actually used, while the milligram figure Ramos quotes alongside corresponds to the correct, weaker strength - the Europe PMC title and methods name the weaker preparation. Second, Fulling measured precipitate accumulating with incubation time to a plateau at 20 minutes even at its lowest bicarbonate amount, where Ramos looked for five minutes only; Ramos attributes the disagreement between the two to methodology. Third, Fulling's own conclusion turns on that window rather than on clarity at time zero. Together the two set the observation window, not the bicarbonate quantity, as the variable that decides whether a partly buffered ropivacaine is reported as clear - which is why D017 is refuted as worded while the question of persistence is untouched.
quote_from_abstract: Even with a low dose of bicarbonate ([dose figure omitted] bicarbonate/[dose figure omitted] ropivacaine), precipitation increased with time of incubation, reaching a plateau at 20 minutes.

citation: Lambert DH. Clinical value of adding sodium bicarbonate to local anesthetics. Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine 2002;27(3):328-9; author reply 329-30. DOI 10.1053/rapm.2002.31931
found_in_paper: Not cited by Ramos - it is a published Letter/Comment ON Ramos with an author reply, found on the Europe PMC record for Ramos (commentCorrection, type 'Comment in') and then fetched (engine: europepmc, query EXT_ID:12016613).
what_it_shows: A post-publication exchange about the Ramos result itself, which is the only such exchange attached to any of the four studies bearing on D017. It could sharpen or qualify the verdict, so it was pursued. Europe PMC carries no abstract for it and its only full-text link is marked subscription-required, so it was not read and nothing from it is relied on. Recorded as an unresolved loose end: a free legitimate copy was not found, no account was created, and no paywall was crossed. It is cited nowhere in the Notion record either.

citation: Guerrier G, Boutboul D, Chanat C, Samama CM, Baillard C. Bicarbonate-buffered ropivacaine-mepivacaine solution for medial caruncle anaesthesia. Anaesthesia Critical Care & Pain Medicine 2017;36(4):219-221. DOI 10.1016/j.accpm.2016.09.007
found_in_paper: Not cited by Ramos. Already named in claim D018's existing reason; retrieved here while confirming the universe of alkalinized-ropivacaine studies (engine: europepmc, query TITLE_ABS:("alkalinized ropivacaine" OR "alkalinised ropivacaine" OR "alkalinization of ropivacaine" OR "buffered ropivacaine"), hitCount 3 - the three being Fulling 2000, Ramos 2001 and this).
what_it_shows: A prospective, monocentric, double-blind randomised controlled trial in 40 consecutive eye-surgery patients, comparing self-reported injection pain between a plain ropivacaine-mepivacaine mixture at pH 5.9 and the same mixture pH-adjusted to 7.0 with bicarbonate; injection pain was significantly lower in the buffered group. It does not decide D017, because it reports nothing at all about precipitate or the appearance of the solution, which is D017's outcome element, and because the ropivacaine is diluted into a mepivacaine mixture rather than buffered on its own. It does not change D018 either, which already names it. Recorded here because it is the third and last member of the alkalinized-ropivacaine literature and because it shows a buffered ropivacaine-containing solution taken all the way to pH 7.0 and injected into patients, which is well above the pH at which plain ropivacaine is reported to precipitate - a tension the record does not currently note, and one the mepivacaine in the mixture probably explains.
quote_from_abstract: This prospective, monocentric, double blind, randomised, controlled trial involved 40 consecutive patients who received either a standard local anaesthetic solution

citation: Mumford JM, Gray TC. Dental trial of carbocaine; a new local anaesthetic. Br J Anaesth 1957;29(5):210-216
found_in_paper: Cited in the discussion of S-686-25, with Berling 1958, for mepivacaine used alone being successful in dental anaesthesia but having 'a rather short duration of action'.
what_it_shows: A human dental trial of mepivacaine (Carbocaine) against lidocaine, indexed under Humans, Mepivacaine, Lidocaine and Anesthesia, Local. It is a mouth-tissue study, not a skin study, so it does not add to the count of studies timing mepivacaine in skin; it matters because it is one of the two sources Reynolds reads as showing mepivacaine's duration is short, which cuts against a 2.5-hour mepivacaine figure. Europe PMC holds no abstract (pre-1966 citation). A free full text is listed at the publisher DOI via Unpaywall. Engine: Europe PMC (TITLE search).

citation: Rubin AP, Lawson DI. A controlled trial of bupivacaine. A comparison with lignocaine. Anaesthesia 1968;23(3):327-330
found_in_paper: Cited in the discussion of S-686-25 as evidence that bupivacaine produces much more prolonged regional block analgesia than lignocaine, the contrast used to warn against extrapolating intradermal duration to other routes.
what_it_shows: A randomised controlled trial comparing bupivacaine with lignocaine, indexed under Anesthesia, Spinal and Time Factors. It is a nerve-trunk/neuraxial duration comparison, not a skin measurement, so it does not bear on the wheal-volume duration claims except as the non-skin figure those claims are contrasted with. Europe PMC holds no abstract; a free PDF is listed via Unpaywall. Engine: Europe PMC (TITLE search).
engine_query: TITLE:"controlled trial of bupivacaine" AND PUB_YEAR:1968

citation: Watt MJ, Ross DM, Atkinson RS. A double-blind trial of bupivacaine and lignocaine. Latency and duration in extradural blockade. Anaesthesia 1968;23(3):331-337
found_in_paper: Cited alongside Rubin and Lawson in the discussion of S-686-25 for bupivacaine's prolonged block by a non-intradermal route.
what_it_shows: A randomised double-blind trial of latency and duration of extradural blockade with bupivacaine against lignocaine. Extradural, not skin, so again only the contrast route. Europe PMC holds no abstract; a free PDF is listed via Unpaywall. Engine: Europe PMC (TITLE search).
engine_query: TITLE:"double-blind trial of bupivacaine and lignocaine"

citation: Fairley JW, Reynolds F. An intradermal study of the local anaesthetic and vascular effects of the isomers of mepivacaine. Br J Anaesth 1981;53(11):1211-1216
found_in_paper: Not cited by S-686-25, which predates it; looked up to place S-686-25 in the Reynolds intradermal series, because the mepivacaine-wheals page calls this paper the only study that measured mepivacaine in human skin by pinprick over an intradermal bleb.; S-686-40 reference list and discussion (cited for the finding that L(+) mepivacaine's longer action was not associated with greater vasoconstriction)
what_it_shows: A double-blind intradermal study in 23 fit volunteers of L(+), D(-) and racemic mepivacaine plus saline, at a range of concentrations, with analgesia to pinprick tested at 5-min intervals until full recovery - the same method as S-686-25 but five years later, so S-686-25 is the earlier measurement of mepivacaine in human skin by that test. It also reports human intradermal log dose-duration plots for mepivacaine, so the concentration-duration slopes are not unique to Willatts 1985. Its finding that duration rose with concentration in the low range is compatible with the flat 1-3% relationship in S-686-25 if the curve plateaus above about 1%. Engine: Europe PMC (AUTH search).
quote_from_abstract: The duration of action of both isomers increased with concentration between 0.05 and 0.9%, but the L isomer was significantly longer acting than the D at 0.3% and more.
engine_query: AUTH:"Fairley" AND AUTH:"Reynolds" AND (mepivacaine OR intradermal)

citation: Willatts DG, Reynolds F. Comparison of the vasoactivity of amide and ester local anaesthetics. An intradermal study. Br J Anaesth 1985;57(10):1006-1011
found_in_paper: Not cited by S-686-25, which predates it; looked up because it is the source the prilocaine-wheals, mepivacaine-wheals and comparison pages treat as the only or the second intradermal timing of these agents.
what_it_shows: A double-blind intradermal study in 10 volunteers of six agents - procaine, amethocaine, cinchocaine, lignocaine, mepivacaine and prilocaine - reporting duration of action and vascular effects. It is the third, not the first or second, intradermal timing of mepivacaine and prilocaine in human skin once S-686-25 (1976) and Fairley 1981 are counted. Its finding that duration was concentration-dependent for all six drugs disagrees with S-686-25, which found no significant difference in duration across the three concentrations it tested for three agents; the likely reconciliation is that Willatts spanned much lower concentrations where the log dose-duration slope is steep. Engine: Europe PMC (EXT_ID fetch).
quote_from_abstract: Duration of action was concentration-dependent for all six drugs, the slopes of the log dose--duration plots reflecting the observed vasoactivity.

citation: Cederholm I, Evers H, Löfström JB. Skin blood flow after intradermal injection of ropivacaine in various concentrations with and without epinephrine evaluated by laser Doppler flowmetry. Reg Anesth 1992;17(6):322-328
found_in_paper: Reference [3], discussed on page 10 of S-686-28 ('Cederholm et al. [3] concluded in their analysis that ropivacaine in different concentrations with epinephrine additive (1 : 200.000) decrease the vasoconstrictive effect of epinephrine.'). Record fetched from Europe PMC by title search.
what_it_shows: The study that sets the 90-minute boundary the wheal pages assert. Randomised, double-blind, 23 healthy young male non-smoking volunteers, four test sites per volar forearm, intradermal injection of ropivacaine at several concentrations with and without epinephrine, with saline, lidocaine and an untreated area as controls; skin blood flow by laser Doppler flowmetry. Its last reading is at 90 minutes, so it is the right route and the right outcome for W-R005 and it stops exactly where the claim says the literature stops. It therefore supports the claim rather than refuting it, and it is the reason a nerve-block recording running to 24 hours does not close the wheal gap.
quote_from_abstract: Recordings were made at 20, 40, 60, and 90 minutes after intradermal injection

citation: Cederholm I, Evers H, Löfström JB. Effect of intradermal injection of saline or a local anaesthetic agent on skin blood flow - a methodological study in man. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1991;35(3):208-215
found_in_paper: NOT cited by S-686-28. Found by Europe PMC author search while testing W-R005 independently (engine: europepmc).
what_it_shows: A second, independent laser Doppler study of intradermal ropivacaine in human forearm skin, and it also stops at 90 minutes. Randomised, double-blind, 17 healthy young male volunteers, four test sites per volar forearm; Group III (n=12) received intradermal ropivacaine 0.75% and 0.25% alongside bupivacaine and lidocaine, and reported that ropivacaine at clinical concentrations decreased skin blood flow. Because the two laser Doppler wheal studies of ropivacaine both end at 90 minutes, the '90 minutes' in W-R005 is traceable to real recording schedules rather than being an unverified assertion.
quote_from_abstract: Recordings were made at 20, 40, 60 and in Group III also at 90 min after needle insertion or intradermal injection.

citation: Cederholm I, Åkerman B, Evers H. Local analgesic and vascular effects of intradermal ropivacaine and bupivacaine in various concentrations with and without addition of adrenaline in man. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1994;38(4):322-327
found_in_paper: NOT cited by S-686-28 (its sibling, reference [3], is the 1992 paper). Found by Europe PMC author search; it is the 'Cederholm et al., 1994' the pages cite for intradermal ropivacaine duration.
what_it_shows: The third intradermal ropivacaine study in humans, and the one that could most easily have been mistaken for a long wheal flow recording. Randomised, double-blind, 10 healthy young male volunteers, intradermal wheals of ropivacaine and bupivacaine at several concentrations with and without adrenaline, pin-prick for dermal analgesia. Its vascular endpoint is visual inspection of the injected area graded nil / pink / pale, not a flow measurement, so it does not extend the wheal blood-flow record past 90 minutes and leaves W-R005 intact. It is the source of the concentration-duration figures the pages use for intradermal ropivacaine.
quote_from_abstract: Local vascular effects at the injected areas were determined by visual inspection (nil, pink, pale).

citation: Häfner HM, Schmid U, Moehrle M, Strölin A, Breuninger H. Changes in acral blood flux under local application of ropivacaine and lidocaine with and without an adrenaline additive: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study. Clin Hemorheol Microcirc 2008;38(4):279-288

what_it_shows: The study the D001 annotation describes, and the paper my own paper most resembles. Prospective, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, 20 vascularly healthy volunteers, Oberst's-method digital blocks, laser Doppler skin blood flux at the fingerpads followed over 24 hours, with plain ropivacaine, plain lidocaine, lidocaine with adrenaline and saline placebo arms. Plain ropivacaine raised flux by 155.2% with vasodilatation still demonstrable at 24 hours - confirming every figure the Notion annotation gives for it. S-686-28 is the same group repeating the same design on different fingers with epinephrine and tumescent arms added, which is why D001's 'the one' fails: the two are twin studies of the same measurement, not one unique study.
quote_from_abstract: We studied skin blood flux at the fingerpads via laser Doppler flowmetry over the course of 24 hours in a prospective, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study with 20 vascularly healthy test persons following Oberst's-method anesthetic blocks.

citation: Selander D, Sjöstrand J. Longitudinal spread of intraneurally injected local anesthetics. An experimental study of the initial neural distribution following intraneural injections. Acta Anaesthesiol Scand 1978;22(6):622-634
what_it_shows: Reference 14 of Tajiri 1998, cited there for how far an injected local anaesthetic spreads along a nerve, which is the step Tajiri's mechanism argument turns on: if the drug cannot travel from the fibular head to the lumbar root, the relief cannot be explained by the drug reaching the lesion. Verified in Europe PMC: PMID 726868, DOI 10.1111/j.1399-6576.1978.tb01346.x, Journal Article, 82 citing papers. This fills the PMID the paper card left blank rather than guessed. It is an animal distribution study in rabbit sciatic nerve, not a human or a clinical one, and its finding is split by compartment: injections outside the fascicle spread little, injections inside it spread far and in a fifth of cases reached the spinal cord. That split matters for how Tajiri's assumption should be read, because the spread figure Tajiri quotes belongs to the subepineural route rather than to a perineural injection placed near but not into the nerve, which is what Tajiri performed.

citation: Mark LC. Letter: Avoiding the pain of venipuncture. N Engl J Med 1976;294(11):614
what_it_shows: Reference 1 of Wightman and Vaughan 1976, and the source of the proposition the paper was written to test: that physiologic saline is a satisfactory local anaesthetic free of discomfort for venipuncture. Wightman and Vaughan tested it against five other intradermal solutions and rejected it in both directions, reporting that saline alone gave poor to no anaesthesia in most subjects and was the most uncomfortable of the six to inject. It bears on no claim id in claims_all.json, but it is the provenance of any statement that a saline wheal anaesthetises, and it is the counterpart of the Ropivacaine Wheals page's 'Saline was not inert' passage, which reads a larger-volume control infiltration the other way; that is recorded as Notion finding S-686-39-F016.
